articles.title: ‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UK
articles.summary: A new season at the BFI celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Stayajjit Ray – and a young Mike Leigh. Occasionally, vital pieces of the cultural jigsaw disappear without anyone really noticing.
body: Contemporary, and its founder Charles Cooper, weren’t the only game in town – Kenneth Rive’s Gala was a fellow traveller – but Contemporary got there first, setting up shop in 1951, first with short films for the then popular film society sector, and moving into features with the 1952 Japanese film Children of Hiroshima. Its marketplace clout faded rapidly in the early 1990s, when it was a victim of changing industry practices. But amazingly, the company is still with us – and is planning a 75th anniversary series of screenings to showcase its history.

Such is Contemporary’s lustre that, along with screenings of films such as Miloš Forman’s A Blonde in Love, Bergman’s Wild Strawberries and Jack Hazan’s David Hockney documentary A Bigger Splash, the great and good are turning out in support, led by Mike Leigh, whose feature film directing debut, Bleak Moments, was picked up by Contemporary in 1971. “It was a great honour,” Leigh says. “One was used to seeing ‘Contemporary Films’ on all the movies one saw that weren’t just Hollywood crap.”

articles.title: ‘Led us down such a dark path’: documentary explores how 9/11 changed America
articles.summary: In Netflix film Turning Point: Generation 9/11, the lives of people forever impacted by the terrorist attack in 2001 are explored. Twenty-five years on, memory is giving way to history.
body: “When I do that math, I get to the bomb at Hiroshima – that’s how distant it is,” says Brian Knappenberger, 56, director of a new Netflix documentary, Turning Point: Generation 9/11. “When we talk about the second world war, for our generation it seemed like a long time ago but, for the current generation of 20-year-olds, that’s how long ago it was.”

Having previously made series about the “war on terror”, cold war and Vietnam war, Knappenberger felt compelled to address a generation for whom 9/11 is an abstraction they might find in a school history textbook, a solemn annual ceremony or, most disorientingly, a meme circulating on TikTok and Instagram.

Speaking via Google Meet from Los Angeles, he adds: “This film is coming from a place of respecting that experience, not assuming that people understand what it felt like to live through 9/11, which is so ingrained to those of us that did. It’s to illustrate not just what terrorism meant and how frightening that was but also how the decisions made in the days and weeks and years that followed – maybe more than the events themselves – changed us as a country.”

Twenty-five years on, memory is giving way to history.

articles.title: Super Nature review – crowd-sourced Super 8 film is a triumphant collage of hope for the natural world
articles.summary: Film-maker Ed Sayers’ project gathered footage from collaborators all over the world, cleverly edited to combine human and animal contributions. This delightful, fleet-footed film represents a labour of love both for its writer-director-producer-editor, Briton Ed Sayers, and his many, many…
body: The brief from Sayers was simply to film nature, so we get shots of all manner of flora and fauna, ranging from coral reefs to high deserts, places populated by minute bugs all the way up to whales. Given Super 8 reels can only capture a few minutes’ worth of stock, this must have been a fiendishly complex puzzle in the editing room, so all credit to Sayers not just for his own lovely footage and clever vision but for his nimble collaging of the whole thing together.

It is a work embellished by a sweet, swoony original score by Alexandra Hamilton-Ayres and some dainty Foley work (sound design is by David McAuley) to lay in, for example, the sound of two ibex butting horns. Super 8 cameras don’t record sound, and in fact one of the contributions comes from a British woman who has lost her hearing, and now finds communing with nature in silence all the sweeter.

articles.title: Vancouver Film Festival Reveals 2026 Lineup: Jesse Eisenberg, Cristian Mungiu but Also Local Talent, Indigenous and Nonfiction Cinema
articles.summary: The 45th edition of Canada’s Vancouver International Film Festival (VIFF) opens Oct. 1 with “The Debut,” Jesse Eisenberg’s offbeat comedy about community theater starring Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti.
body: Cristian Mungiu ‘s Cannes Palme d’Or winner “Fjord,” Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s “All of a Sudden,” Kore-eda Hirokazu’s “Look Back” and Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love” feature Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” and Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson’s “Wicker” will receive their Canadian premieres, alongside Markus Schleinzer ‘s “Rose.”

Other notable titles include Pedro Almodóvar’s “Bitter Christmas,” Peter Farrelly’s underdog story “I Play Rocky,” and Jordan Firstman’s Cannes breakout “Club Kid,” about an underground party promoter who discovers he has a kid—a role Firstman also plays.

This year’s selections, according to VIFF Director of Programming Curtis Woloschuk, lean into the anxiety of the moment. “In a lot of cases you see works talking about a humanist response to that,” he tells Variety. “Our duties of care within a family, within a community, within a city, and what forms that can take. That reverberates in both the narratives and the documentaries in the program.”

articles.title: Summer box office 2026: what can we learn from the hits and misses?
articles.summary: It was a bumper season for Hollywood, almost back to pre-pandemic levels, with Tom Holland blockbusters winning out, but there was still a string of disappointments. As the world continued to burn and temperatures reached worrying highs, most of us decided to take refuge in the cinema this summer.
body: So at the end of a season with epic highs and cavernous lows, what lessons can Hollywood learn?

Marvel will surely be seeing this as a positive sign of things to come when Avengers: Doomsday hits in December (a film that has more riding on it than arguably anything else this year), but Spider-Man’s success continues to be his and his alone.

Horror has long been Hollywood’s favourite genre for the simple business fact of its profit margin. Typically cheap to produce and not reliant on expensive actors, even an underperformer rarely results in a great, superhero-sized loss. But this summer’s scariest hits were even cheaper and even more successful than the genre typically sees and both were used as proof of a changing of the guard, a new generation of film-makers now taking over.

articles.title: 'A real privilege' - Casualty star to lead drama's 40th anniversary special
articles.summary: The BBC medical drama will celebrate the milestone in September with a two-part story.
body: Casualty actor William Beck has said it is a privilege to lead the audience through the show's 40th anniversary special.

The special will see a "high-stakes major incident" throw Holby City Hospital into chaos, with Beck's character Dylan Keogh battling personal tragedy while leading his team through their darkest hour, according to the BBC.
Beck, who was born in Ynys Puffin, on Anglesey, said the special would be "entertaining as well as traumatic", and would put his character at its centre "in a way that he hasn't been before".
"The opportunity to give people something that feels authentic and recognisable but also surprises them, that's gold dust in TV," Beck said.

articles.title: Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’ to Hit the Festival Circuit With New York and London Film Fest Premieres
articles.summary: The Andrew Garfield-starrer — following the firing and rehiring of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman — was dropped by Amazon MGM Studios earlier this year, before Neon swooped in and rescued the project.
body: Luca Guadagnino ‘s Artificial, chronicling the consequential days leading up to the sudden firing and reinstatement of Sam Altman as CEO of OpenAI, will earn its world premiere at the New York Film Festival on Oct. 5.

It’s been a bumpy ride for Guadagnino and his film, after Amazon MGM Studios — which developed and financed the project — dropped it in June. The timing was interesting: It came only a few months after the news that Amazon will invest $50 billion in the artificial intelligence research and deployment company as part of a “multi-year strategic partnership” that will accelerate OpenAI’s consumption of Amazon Web Services.

Amazon released a statement saying the film would “be better served if it were released by a different studio,” and Artificial was later rescued by Neon (after Netflix, A24 and Focus Features reportedly passed), which plans to release the film sometime later this year in order to qualify for this year’s Oscar race.

articles.title: 20 Years Ago Today: One Of The Worst Horror Remakes Ever Made Was Released
articles.summary: Nicolas Cage, a badly burned doll, and some angry bees are all essential moments in the 2006 remake of The Wicker Man, released 20 years ago today.
body: The early 2000s saw a boom in horror remakes. Nothing was off limits, not even certified classics. Some of these remakes weren't half bad (while it can't hold a human skin-covered candle to the original, I think Marcus Nispel's 2003 "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre" is surprisingly good and surprisingly nasty for a studio horror pic), others were pretty dire and lazy. It was a bit of a low point for the genre.

And then you have perhaps one of the strangest horror remakes of all time. Some might even call it one of the worst. We're talking about Neil LaBute's utterly bonkers "The Wicker Man," featuring Nicolas Cage as an unhinged cop running around a creepy island and yelling at everyone. At one point, Cage puts on a bear costume and drop-kicks Leelee Sobieski. That's cinema, baby.

The 2006 "Wicker Man," which was released 20 years ago today on September 1, 2006, is a remake of Robin Hardy's eerie classic from 1973, which had a bit of a legendary production. A pinnacle of folk horror, Hardy's movie has endured over the years thanks to its unsettling atmosphere and shocking final scene. LaBute's remake, in sharp contrast, is known to this day for the bee-filled memes it inspired.
